_meta: One tiny treatment effect measured at two sample sizes, used to show why statistical significance is not the same as practical importance -- with a large enough sample a trivially small effect becomes statistically significant while remaining too small to matter. baseline_rate is the control conversion rate (0.50). effect is the true absolute lift of the treatment (0.002 = 0.2 percentage points) -- the SAME real effect at every sample size. practical_threshold is the smallest lift the team considers worth shipping (0.01 = 1 percentage point); an effect below it is not worth acting on even if real. sample_sizes are the per-arm sample sizes to evaluate: 1000 (a modest test) and 1000000 (a huge one). The standard error of the difference shrinks as the sample grows (SE = sqrt(2*p*(1-p)/n)), so the z-statistic (effect / SE) grows with n even though the effect itself never changes: at n=1000 the 0.2pp lift is nowhere near significant, at n=1000000 the identical 0.2pp lift is comfortably significant (p well below 0.05). But the effect is 0.2pp either way -- below the 1pp practical threshold -- so it is never worth shipping. At the large n the confidence interval excludes zero (significant) yet lies entirely below the practical threshold, the clean picture of a real-but-negligible effect. baseline_rate, effect, practical_threshold, and sample_sizes are the fixture; every standard error, z, p-value, and confidence interval is computed.
